extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers in the history and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Discussing and evaluating competing foundational positions (intuitionism vs formalism) in twentieth-century mathematics, including criteria for acceptable proofs, axioms, and consistency arguments. The page is a historical/philosophical overview rather than a technical how-to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of the law of excluded middle
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the law of excluded middle (LEM) is a valid principle of inference, especially when extended over infinite domains (Cantor's 'completed infinite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer rejects the unrestricted use of LEM over infinite sets, arguing it is valid only for finite systems; Hilbert defends LEM as essential to axiomatic formalism. Evaluation hinges on whether proofs invoke LEM over completed infinities and whether that invocation is philosophically or mathematically justified. (Article quotes Hilbert's defense and Brouwer's critique and notes Hilbert's remark comparing prohibiting LEM to prohibiting a boxer the use of his fists.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructibility (requirement for constructive proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether existence claims and other proofs exhibit constructibility—i.e., provide a method to actually construct the object claimed to exist rather than only proving existence indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer and intuitionists require constructive proofs; Hilbert's 'existence proofs' that eliminate explicit constructions are criticized for losing constructibility. The trade-off is noted: existence proofs give brevity and economy of thought but do not produce mathematical objects. Kleene's work and intuitionistic disallowance of certain logical laws (e.g., double negation elimination) are cited as formal reflections of this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the 'completed infinite' (Cantorian infinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it is acceptable to adopt Cantor's notion of a 'completed infinite' in foundations and to extend logical principles (like LEM) across infinite totalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer characterized Hilbert's wholesale adoption of the completed infinite as 'thoughtless'; critics argue that extrapolating finite logical principles to completed infinite domains is unjustified. Evaluations should check for tacit appeals to totalities and whether arguments legitimately generalize from finite to infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of axioms: consistency versus intuitive truth
rubrics_metrics.description: What justifies selecting a set of axioms: mere formal consistency, or axioms grounded in mathematical intuition/phenomenology?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's formalism treats axioms as arbitrary declarations so long as they are consistent; Weyl and others argue consistency is necessary but not sufficient and that axioms should reflect intuitive mathematical truths. Assessments should consider whether axioms are being chosen solely for formal properties or also for their intuitive/semantic fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of tacit assumptions and attention to semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a formal development genuinely avoids tacit assumptions about meaning, or whether it covertly relies on semantics/tacit knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert claimed his system admitted no tacit assumptions, but critics (and Breger citing Polanyi) argue mathematics presupposes tacit knowledge about symbols and their use. Evaluators should look for hidden semantic commitments behind formal manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a generalized consistency proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A consistency proof intended to settle the foundations must be non-circular and valid when applied to all formulas (including the proof procedure itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's second problem sought a generalized proof P that, given any theorem T (including P itself), decides provability. Critics (Poincaré, Weyl) point out circularity dangers and that such a proof would require uses of LEM over all formulas and all assignments, which intuitionists reject. Evaluation should test for implicit circularity (e.g., use of formal induction as a premise) and for whether the proof treats 'all formulas' legitimately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of induction used (formal vs intuitive) and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the argument relies on formal (Peano-style) induction or on intuitive, step-by-step induction, and whether that reliance is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré and others distinguish 'animal-logic' induction from formal induction and argue Hilbert tacitly assumed formal induction, risking circularity. Kleene's distinctions among induction rule, inductive definition, and definition by induction clarify acceptable uses. Evaluations should identify which induction is used and whether it presumes a totality of infinite objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of reductio ad absurdum extended over the infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether proofs by contradiction that range over infinite domains (reductions to absurdity extended over the infinite) are legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert used reductio ad absurdum extended over the infinite in existence proofs; Brouwer objected because such methods may rely on LEM and fail to provide constructions. Assessments should check whether reductio is being used in a way that bypasses constructive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which formalization reduces mathematics to symbol manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether treating mathematics as a 'game with formulas' (pure formal manipulation) is an acceptable conception of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weyl criticized Hilbert's formalization for turning mathematics into formula play, questioning what guides the choice of rules. Evaluations should consider whether the formal system preserves mathematical meaning and creativity or unduly mechanizes mathematics into rule-following without semantic grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of constructive metamathematical methods (e.g., recursion, numeralization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether metamathematical results are presented in a manner that is constructive/intutionistically acceptable (for instance, using primitive recursion and Gödel numeralization rather than non-constructive schemata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel took pains to show aspects of his results are 'constructive' by numeralizing formulae and using primitive recursion; such techniques make results more acceptable to intuitionists. Evaluation should note whether proofs/arguments use recursion and explicit constructions rather than appeals to abstract formal principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and scholarly conduct reflecting philosophical differences
rubrics_metrics.description: How editorial policies and scholarly recognition should be handled when foundational disagreements affect publication and authorship credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hilbert–Brouwer dispute manifested in the removal of Brouwer from Mathematische Annalen's editorial board; Brouwer complained about polemics and lack of proper mention of authorship. As a norm, editorial practice should recognize authorship and avoid letting philosophical conflicts produce unfair editorial action or suppression.
